findings.summary:
I reviewed commit f05a33a against approved CODEX-04-B (spec blob 14e79c18, authorized in the execution ledger; prerequisites 04-A, 03-B and 01-B are done). I also checked engineering v1.2 (digest 02adc2e0…) including its README, design, module guide and review notes; AGENTS, GOVERNANCE, SOURCE_OF_TRUTH and APPROVALS; all of PROJECT_CONTEXT v1.96, read in sections through the end of the file; PRODUCT_V1 and PRODUCT_DECISIONS; WM-04; and the full 00-B contracts and 00-C screen map. All three acceptance criteria are met, with real evidence:
- **Atomic booking:** one locked transaction does the eligibility hold, the core booking and its bucket mapping, and the immutable receipt. The 0-for-2 races on the last slot and the last allowance unit end as acknowledged plus no_capacity, or acknowledged plus quota_full, and the released/completed lifecycle is exercised.
- **Deadline:** the server sets the original receipt once, at whole-second precision, and the due time is exactly 24 hours (86,400 s) later. The receipt survives a lost reply, a reload, a 25-hour wait and a new bucket. Same-key retries return the identical receipt.
- **No capacity:** the result carries no receipt, the source stays saved and the clock stays null, and the UI offers an explicit Keep saved-only choice.

Controller evidence on the reviewed tree: 101/101 tests pass, the build passes, protected probes pass, and the CUA observation covers all eight native scenarios. The unresolved gates stay open (G-E03, the 11-C capacity cap, the scheduler, the operator alert), and DECISION-033 is applied as written. Remaining findings are minor or nits.

findings.title: Last-slot race evidence is in-process serialization, not DB lock contention
findings.problem: A module-level `tail` promise chain (`serial`) runs every eligibility, submit, status and reconcile call one at a time, and every service instance in the process shares that chain. PGlite is also single-connection. So the tests and probe described as 'across service instances' or 'two independent instances' never contend for the global bucket's FOR UPDATE row lock. AC1's no-overbooking claim is shown for the local single-process synthetic stack only. The real-Postgres, multi-connection path of `available()` under the bucket lock has not been exercised. The report's limitations partly disclose this; the test names overstate it.
findings.fix_check: Test names or REPORT limitations say the race is serialized in-process and on single-connection PGlite. Alternatively, a multi-connection Postgres race (when 00-F/G-E01 allows it) shows exactly one booking with the module chain bypassed.

findings.title: Kernel hold locks households row after request/entitlement/bucket locks
findings.problem: scope() locks service_consents and child profiles. submit then locks wonder_requests, entitlements, periods and the global bucket before calling kernel.apply. apply then runs `SELECT … FROM households … FOR UPDATE` (entitlements.mjs:62), taking the household level after later levels are already held. Architecture v1.2 says never to acquire an earlier lock level after a later one. With real multi-connection Postgres this risks deadlocking against writers that take households first. withSession's bounded retry would mask that, but it is not the specified order.
findings.fix_check: scope() (or the submit transaction) locks the households row before consent/request/entitlement/bucket. Alternatively, the report records the ordering exception and why it cannot deadlock.

findings.title: Conflict and stale-version outcomes give poor UI recovery
findings.problem: source() reports a stale or non-latest wonder version as 'denied'. The UI treats 403 as lost access and clears the selected child. A 409 conflict on a fresh submit (for example, an offer_version mismatch after the period changed) lands in the generic catch. That path keeps the intent and offers 'Retry original production request', which will conflict every time until the page is reloaded. No booking or clock is affected; this is recovery UX only.
findings.fix_check: A 409 on a new (never-committed) submission clears the RAM intent and asks the user to review eligibility again. A stale source version returns a conflict rather than an access denial.

findings.title: Eligibility can call an already-requested wonder 'eligible'
findings.problem: source() does not check `original_received_at`, so eligibility() can report status 'eligible' for a wonder that already has a production command; submit then rejects it with a conflict. The UI's saved list filters these wonders out, so this shows only through direct API use. Eligibility is advisory, so nothing wrong is booked.
findings.fix_check: eligibility() returns a non-eligible status when the request already has an original receipt or a production command.

findings.title: Status ledger and report header are stale relative to the reviewed commit
findings.problem: The status file says state=blocked with result_commit 0b700d0. The opening REPORT section still says 'No revision-2 check was run', even though the appended controller sections record passing checks on this tree. Both are controller-managed and historically labelled, but an acceptance step could pin the wrong revision from them.
findings.fix_check: On acceptance, the controller updates result_commit, state and accepted_by to the exact merged commit. The report keeps the historical header but is clearly superseded by the appended evidence.
